lessons.title: Whole Fruit Preserves: Cherries and Figs
lessons.body: Whole fruit preserves keep the fruit intact, suspended in a thick syrup. In Africa, cherries grow in cool highlands like Kenya's Rift Valley and South Africa's Free State. Figs thrive in warmer, drier areas such as Morocco, Egypt, and Tunisia. For cherries, choose firm, ripe fruit. Remove stems but keep pits for better shape, or pit them if you prefer. For figs, pick fully ripe but not mushy. Wash and pat dry. For every 1 kg of fruit, use 800 g of white sugar and 2 tablespoons of lemon juice. Lemon juice adds acid for set and brightens colour. Layer fruit and sugar in a bowl, cover, and refrigerate for 12 hours. This draws out juice. Next day, pour everything into a wide, heavy pot. Add lemon juice. Bring to a boil slowly, stirring gently. Skim foam. Cook at a rolling boil until a candy thermometer reads 105Â°C (221Â°F), about 20â30 minutes. Stir only occasionally to avoid breaking fruit. Test set by placing a spoonful on a cold plate; it should wrinkle when pushed. For figs, add 1 teaspoon of vanilla or a stick of cinnamon for warmth. Ladle hot preserves into sterilised jars, leaving 1 cm headspace. Wipe rims, seal, and process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes. Store in a cool, dark place. Use within 12 months. Enjoy on toast, with cheese, or as a gift.

lessons.title: Conserves with Nuts and Dried Fruits
lessons.body: Conserves are jam-like mixtures that include nuts and dried fruits, giving them a rich, chunky texture. They are popular in North Africa and the Middle East, where dried apricots, dates, and almonds are abundant. Start with 1 kg of fresh fruit (such as peaches, pears, or plums), 500 g of mixed dried fruit (raisins, chopped dates, apricots), and 200 g of nuts (walnuts, almonds, or pecans). You also need 1 kg of sugar, 2 tablespoons of lemon juice, and 1 teaspoon of ground cinnamon or ginger. Peel and chop fresh fruit. Soak dried fruit in warm water for 30 minutes, then drain. In a large pot, combine fresh fruit, dried fruit, sugar, and lemon juice. Cook over medium heat, stirring until sugar dissolves. Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 30 minutes, stirring often to prevent sticking. Add nuts and spices. Continue cooking until thick, about 15â20 minutes more. The mixture should mound on a spoon. Test set by freezing a small plate; place a spoonful on it and check if it gels after 1 minute. If not, cook 5 more minutes. Ladle into sterilised jars, leaving 1 cm headspace. Remove air bubbles with a knife. Seal and process in a boiling water bath for 15 minutes. This conserve pairs well with bread, yoghurt, or as a filling for pastries. Store in a cool, dark place for up to 1 year.

lessons.title: Slow-Cooked Apple and Pear Butters
lessons.body: Fruit butters are smooth, thick spreads made by slow-cooking fruit pulp with sugar and spices until dark and creamy. They are ideal for using up windfall apples and pears, common in temperate regions of Africa like the High Atlas in Morocco or the Drakensberg in South Africa. You need 2 kg of apples or pears, 500 g of sugar, 1 teaspoon of ground cinnamon, Â½ teaspoon of ground cloves, and 2 tablespoons of lemon juice. Wash, peel, core, and chop the fruit. Place in a heavy pot with 250 ml of water. Cook over low heat until soft, about 30 minutes. Mash or blend until smooth. Return to pot. Add sugar, spices, and lemon juice. Stir well. Cook uncovered over very low heat for 1.5 to 2 hours, stirring every 10 minutes to prevent burning. The butter is ready when a spoonful placed on a cold plate holds its shape and no liquid separates. It should be thick and spreadable. For a deeper flavour, you can add 1 tablespoon of molasses or dark honey. Sterilise jars by boiling them for 10 minutes. Fill hot jars with hot butter, leaving 1 cm headspace. Wipe rims, seal, and process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes. Cool, label, and store in a cool, dark place for up to 6 months. Refrigerate after opening. Great on toast, pancakes, or stirred into porridge.

lessons.title: Pumpkin and Sweet Potato Butter
lessons.body: Pumpkin and sweet potato butters are nutritious, naturally sweet spreads that use abundant African crops. Pumpkins grow across the continent, and sweet potatoes are a staple in many countries. This butter is a good way to preserve surplus harvest. You need 1.5 kg of pumpkin or sweet potato (or a mix), 400 g of sugar, 1 teaspoon of ground ginger, Â½ teaspoon of ground nutmeg, 1 teaspoon of ground cinnamon, and 3 tablespoons of lemon juice. Peel, seed, and cube the pumpkin or sweet potato. Steam or boil until very soft, about 20 minutes. Drain well and mash or blend until smooth. In a heavy pot, combine the puree, sugar, spices, and lemon juice. Cook over low heat, stirring frequently, for 1 to 1.5 hours. The mixture will thicken and darken. Be careful: it can splatter. Use a splatter guard or long spoon. It is ready when a spoonful mounds on a cold plate and no water oozes out. For a richer flavour, add 2 tablespoons of butter or coconut oil at the end. Sterilise jars. Fill hot jars with hot butter, leaving 1 cm headspace. Remove air bubbles. Seal and process in a boiling water bath for 15 minutes. Store in a cool, dark place for up to 6 months. This butter is excellent on bread, in muffins, or as a side with roasted meats. It also makes a thoughtful gift.

lessons.title: Tropical Fruit Conserves: Mango and Pineapple
lessons.body: Tropical fruit conserves capture the vibrant flavours of mango and pineapple, which are plentiful in West, East, and Central Africa. These fruits are high in pectin and acid, making them excellent for conserves. For a mixed conserve, use 1 kg of ripe mango flesh (about 3 large mangoes), 1 kg of fresh pineapple chunks, 800 g of sugar, 2 tablespoons of lime juice, and 1 teaspoon of grated fresh ginger. Peel and chop mangoes and pineapple into bite-sized pieces. In a large pot, combine fruit, sugar, lime juice, and ginger. Let sit for 1 hour to draw out juices. Then bring to a boil over medium heat, stirring until sugar dissolves. Cook at a rolling boil for 25â35 minutes, stirring occasionally. Skim foam. The conserve is ready when it thickens and a spoonful on a cold plate wrinkles when pushed. For a smoother texture, mash some fruit with a potato masher. You can also add 100 g of chopped toasted coconut or macadamia nuts in the last 5 minutes for crunch. Ladle into sterilised jars, leaving 1 cm headspace. Wipe rims, seal, and process in a boiling water bath for 15 minutes. Store in a cool, dark place for up to 1 year. This conserve is delicious on toast, with yogurt, or as a glaze for grilled chicken or fish.

lessons.title: Spiced Fruit Butters for Fall
lessons.body: Fall fruit butters use late-season fruits like apples, pears, quinces, and plums, combined with warm spices. In Africa, quinces grow in Mediterranean climates, and plums in cooler highlands. This butter is perfect for preserving the autumn harvest. You need 2 kg of mixed fruit (apples, pears, plums, quinces), 500 g of sugar, 1 tablespoon of ground cinnamon, 1 teaspoon of ground cloves, 1 teaspoon of ground allspice, and 2 tablespoons of lemon juice. Wash, peel, core, and chop the fruit. Quinces are hard; cook them first for 20 minutes before adding other fruits. Place all fruit in a heavy pot with 250 ml of water. Cook until soft, about 30 minutes. Mash or blend until smooth. Return to pot. Add sugar, spices, and lemon juice. Cook over low heat for 1.5 to 2 hours, stirring every 10 minutes. The butter is ready when it is thick, glossy, and a spoonful holds its shape on a cold plate. For a smoky note, add Â½ teaspoon of smoked paprika. Sterilise jars. Fill hot jars with hot butter, leaving 1 cm headspace. Remove air bubbles. Seal and process in a boiling water bath for 10 minutes. Store in a cool, dark place for up to 6 months. This spiced butter is wonderful on toast, scones, or stirred into oatmeal. It also makes a great gift during holidays.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Preserves, Conserves & Fruit Butters

This reference sheet consolidates the practical numbers, ratios and process controls you need to produce whole fruit preserves, conserves and fruit butters at a small commercial scale. It is written for African agribusinesses working with local and seasonal fruit â cherries and figs in the highlands, mangoes and pineapples on the coast, apples and pears in temperate zones, and pumpkins and sweet potatoes almost everywhere. The goal is repeatable batches, safe shelf-stable products, and a costed recipe you can price for profit.

1. Core Formula: The Four Controls

Every preserve, conserve and butter is governed by four measurable controls. Get these right and your product will be safe, stable and consistent â the foundation of a sellable brand.

  • Acidity (pH): Target pH â¤ 3.5 for safe boiling-water-bath processing. Most fruits qualify naturally; add lemon juice or citric acid when working with low-acid additions like pumpkin, sweet potato or over-ripe mango.
  • Sugar (Brix): Finished soluble solids of 65â68Â°Brix for preserves and conserves; 60â65Â°Brix for butters. Below 60Â°Brix, water activity rises and mould risk increases sharply.
  • Pectin / solids: Preserves need a set; butters rely on long cooking to thicken. Test set with the plate or spoon method before filling.
  • Heat & seal: Boiling-water-bath process jars for 10â15 minutes (adjust for altitude). Use new lids; check the seal after cooling.

2. Ingredient Ratios by Product Type

Table 1: Working ratios per 1 kg prepared fruit (small-batch commercial)
Product Sugar Acid (lemon juice) Pectin Target Brix Yield (approx.)
Whole cherry preserve700â800 g30 ml0â4 g (if fruit is low-pectin)65â68Â°1.6â1.8 kg
Fig preserve600â700 g40 ml0â3 g65â68Â°1.5â1.7 kg
Mixed fruit conserve550â650 g40 ml4â6 g65â68Â°1.6â1.9 kg
Apple / pear butter400â500 g30 mlNone60â65Â°1.2â1.4 kg
Pumpkin / sweet potato butter450â550 g50 mlNone60â65Â°1.2â1.5 kg
Mango / pineapple conserve550â650 g40â50 ml3â5 g65â68Â°1.6â1.8 kg

Sources: ratios consolidated from FAO, Fruit and Vegetable Processing (1995); University of Georgia Extension, So Easy to Preserve (2014); and USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning (2015). Adjust to local fruit sugar content â always verify with a refractometer.

3. Process Parameters: Time, Temperature, Yield

Table 2: Process control by product family
Parameter Preserves Conserves Fruit Butters
Cook temperature104â106Â°C104â106Â°C98â102Â°C (slow simmer)
Cook time20â40 min30â50 min60â120 min
StirringGentle, occasionalRegularFrequent (prevents scorch)
Set testPlate / spoonPlate / spoonMound on cold plate
Jar fill temp85â90Â°C85â90Â°C85â90Â°C
Water-bath process10â15 min10â15 min10â15 min
Shelf life (sealed)12â18 months12â18 months12â18 months
After opening3â4 weeks (fridge)3â4 weeks (fridge)3â4 weeks (fridge)

Sources: National Center for Home Food Preservation (nchfp.uga.edu, 2023); USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, Guide 2 (2015); FAO Fruit and Vegetable Processing (1995). Altitude adjustment: add 1 minute per 300 m above 1,000 m.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Botulism & Spoilage Risk

Low-acid additions (pumpkin, sweet potato, over-ripe mango, fig) can push pH above 4.6. Never sell or store a boiling-water-bath product with pH > 4.6 â Clostridium botulinum spores can germinate and produce lethal toxin. Always measure pH with a calibrated meter or test strips before filling. If pH is above 4.6, add citric acid or lemon juice until pH â¤ 3.5, or use a pressure canner. Discard any jar with a bulging lid, off-odour, mould, or a failed seal â do not taste-test. Use new lids every batch; never reuse lids. Keep records of pH, Brix and process time for every batch for traceability and food-safety compliance.

4. Africa Context: Sourcing & Costing Notes

Your margin lives in sourcing and yield, not in the cooking. Key practical points for African producers:

  • Cherries & figs: High-value, short-season crops. In Kenya, Ethiopia and South Africa, buy at peak gluts and process immediately. Figs are fragile â process within 12 hours of harvest.
  • Mango & pineapple: Abundant in West and East Africa. Use ripe-but-firm fruit; over-ripe fruit lowers pH naturally but reduces piece integrity for conserves. Pineapple cores and mango cheeks are ideal for butters and conserves.
  • Apple & pear: Temperate zones (South Africa, Morocco, Kenya highlands). Culls and windfalls are perfect for butters â cost per kg can drop 40â60%.
  • Pumpkin & sweet potato: Locally abundant, low cost, high yield. Excellent entry-level butter products for local and regional markets.
  • Sugar: Often the largest input cost. Buy in bulk (50 kg bags) and negotiate with local millers. Consider partial sugar replacement with honey or fruit juice concentrate where regulations allow â but recalculate Brix.
  • Packaging: Glass jars are reusable but heavy for transport. PET jars reduce breakage and freight cost for regional distribution.

5. Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Weigh everything. Record fruit, sugar, acid and pectin in grams per batch.
  2. Check pH of the fruit base before cooking; add acid if above 3.5.
  3. Sterilise jars (boiling water, 10 min) and use new lids every batch.
  4. Cook to temperature â 104â106Â°C for preserves/conserves, 98â102Â°C for butters.
  5. Test the set on a cold plate before filling; under-set product will not keep.
  6. Fill hot (85â90Â°C) leaving 6 mm headspace; remove air bubbles.
  7. Water-bath process 10â15 min (plus altitude adjustment); cool undisturbed 12â24 h.
  8. Verify seals, label with batch date, pH and Brix â and keep the record.

6. Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • National Center for Home Food Preservation (NCHFP) â complete, research-based guides for jams, preserves, conserves and butters.
  • FAO â Fruit and Vegetable Processing (Agricultural Services Bulletin 119) â free full text on small-scale processing in developing countries.
  • FAO â Small-scale Fruit and Vegetable Processing and Products â practical enterprise guide with costing and marketing sections.
  • USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning â authoritative process times and safety standards (available via NIFA and NCHFP).
  • WHO/FAO â Codex Alimentarius: Standard for Jams, Jellies and Marmalades (CODEX STAN 296-2009) â the international legal reference for labelling and composition if you export.

quiz.q: What is the recommended sugar-to-fruit ratio for whole fruit preserves?
options: A) 1 kg fruit to 500 g sugar
B) 1 kg fruit to 800 g sugar
C) 1 kg fruit to 1.2 kg sugar
D) 1 kg fruit to 300 g sugar
quiz.explanation: The lesson specifies 800 g of sugar per 1 kg of fruit for whole fruit preserves.

quiz.q: Why is lemon juice added to whole fruit preserves?
options: C) To add acid for set and brighten colour
quiz.explanation: Lemon juice provides acid needed for gelling and helps maintain bright colour.

quiz.q: What temperature should whole fruit preserves reach for a good set?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states a candy thermometer should read 105Â°C (221Â°F).

quiz.q: How long should jars of whole fruit preserves be processed in a boiling water bath?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to process for 10 minutes.

quiz.q: Which of these is a key ingredient in conserves with nuts and dried fruits?
quiz.explanation: Dried fruits like apricots, dates, and raisins are essential in conserves.

quiz.q: What should you do to dried fruit before adding it to a conserve?
quiz.explanation: The lesson instructs to soak dried fruit in warm water for 30 minutes.

quiz.q: How can you test if a conserve is set?
options: B) Place a spoonful on a cold plate
C) Drop a spoonful in water
quiz.explanation: The cold plate test is mentioned for checking set.

quiz.q: What is the processing time for jars of conserve with nuts and dried fruits?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to process for 15 minutes.

quiz.q: What makes fruit butters different from jams?
options: A) They are made with whole fruit
B) They are slow-cooked until smooth and thick
quiz.explanation: Fruit butters are slow-cooked to a smooth, thick consistency.

quiz.q: For apple and pear butter, how long should the fruit be cooked after adding sugar?
quiz.explanation: The lesson states 1.5 to 2 hours of slow cooking.

quiz.q: What is a sign that apple or pear butter is ready?
options: B) A spoonful holds its shape on a cold plate
C) It changes colour to red
quiz.explanation: The cold plate test indicates readiness.

quiz.q: How long should jars of apple or pear butter be processed?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to process for 10 minutes.

quiz.q: What is a key ingredient in pumpkin and sweet potato butter?
quiz.explanation: Ground ginger is listed among the spices.

quiz.q: Why should you use a splatter guard when cooking pumpkin butter?
quiz.explanation: The lesson warns that the mixture can splatter.

quiz.q: How long should pumpkin or sweet potato butter be processed in a boiling water bath?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to process for 15 minutes.

quiz.q: Which fruits are used in tropical fruit conserves?
quiz.explanation: The lesson focuses on mango and pineapple.

quiz.q: What additional ingredient can be added to tropical fruit conserve for crunch?
quiz.explanation: The lesson suggests toasted coconut or macadamia nuts.

quiz.q: How long should mango and pineapple conserve be boiled?
quiz.explanation: The lesson specifies a rolling boil for 25â35 minutes.

quiz.q: What is the processing time for tropical fruit conserve?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to process for 15 minutes.

quiz.q: Which spice is NOT typically used in spiced fruit butters for fall?
quiz.explanation: Turmeric is not mentioned; the others are.

quiz.q: What fruit requires pre-cooking before making fall fruit butter?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says quinces are hard and should be cooked first.

quiz.q: How long should spiced fruit butter be processed in a boiling water bath?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says to process for 10 minutes.

quiz.q: What is a good test for doneness of fruit butters?
options: B) A spoonful holds its shape on a cold plate
quiz.explanation: The cold plate test is used for fruit butters.

quiz.q: What is the recommended headspace when filling jars with preserves?
quiz.explanation: The lessons consistently say to leave 1 cm headspace.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common African region for cherry growing?
quiz.explanation: The lesson mentions Kenya's Rift Valley for cherries.

quiz.q: What is a key step before sealing jars of preserves?
quiz.explanation: Wiping rims ensures a good seal.

quiz.q: How long can whole fruit preserves be stored?
quiz.explanation: The lesson says up to 12 months.

quiz.q: What is a common nut used in conserves?
quiz.explanation: Walnuts are mentioned in the lesson.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of processing jars in a boiling water bath?
quiz.explanation: Boiling water bath ensures a vacuum seal and kills microorganisms.

quiz.q: Which fruit butter is naturally sweet and nutritious, using African staples?
options: B) Pumpkin and sweet potato butter
quiz.explanation: Pumpkin and sweet potato are African staples and make a nutritious butter.
